0.0.n: This is the family name, placed before the given name in Japanese.

0.1.n: 志 is the first character of the given name 志歩; read the name as a whole.

0.2.n: 歩 is the second character of the given name 志歩, not a separate word here.

0.3.n: です politely ends this introduction; the speaker leaves out 私は, meaning I.

1.0.n: This is a family name, followed here by a professional title.

1.1.n: 監督 refers to the team's manager and serves as a title after his name.

1.2.n: は marks Manager Shinjo as the topic being asked about.

1.3.n: 優しい describes kindness; です makes the question polite.

1.4.n: か at the end marks a question.

2.0.n: This family name is followed by the title 監督.

2.1.n: The title follows the family name, unlike the usual English order.

2.2.n: Here はね is topic marker は plus conversational ね, not the verb はねる.

2.4.n: This adjective ends the statement without polite です, giving a casual tone.

2.5.n: よ adds confident emphasis to the speaker's answer.

2.7.n: This casual intensifier is added afterward to strongly emphasize 優しい.

3.0.n: あの is a hesitation filler here, giving the speaker time to organize his thoughts.

3.1.n: This borrowed word refers to public media appearances or coverage.

3.2.n: とか presents the media as one example rather than a complete list.

3.3.n: で marks the setting of his behavior here; it is not a form of だ.

3.4.n: は adds contrast to で, setting public behavior against how he treats the players.

3.6.n: The く-form of 厳しい describes manner; here the speaker pauses and restarts with 厳しいこと.

3.7.n: ね adds a conversational pause and invites the listener to follow along.

3.9.n: 厳しい directly describes the things he says.

3.10.n: こと means the content of what he says, rather than physical objects.

3.11.n: 言っ is the changed stem of 言う used before たり.

3.12.n: たり follows a past-form stem to give an example of an action.

3.13.n: する completes 言ったりする, presenting saying harsh things as an example of his behavior.

3.14.n: けど connects this public image to the contrasting personal experience that follows.

4.0.n: ほんと is a conversational shortening of 本当, used here for emphasis.

4.1.n: 僕ら combines the informal, typically masculine 僕 with ら to include the speaker's group.

4.2.n: と marks the people he talks with.

4.3.n: The plain form of 話す modifies とき to describe when the interaction happens.

4.4.n: とき follows a verb to turn the action into a time expression.

4.5.n: は makes the time he talks with them the topic, contrasting it with media appearances.

4.7.n: いつも describes how consistently he treats them kindly.

4.8.n: 優しい modifies 言葉, describing his choice of words.

4.9.n: 言葉 is the object of かける; the usual object marker を is omitted in this casual speech.

4.10.n: 言葉をかける means address someone; adding てくれる shows the speaker appreciates receiving those words.

4.11.n: し adds this as one reason for the speaker's positive opinion, with more reasons to follow.

5.0.n: 僕ら refers to the speaker and the others in his group.

5.1.n: の links 僕ら to こと; together they still refer to the people themselves.

5.2.n: 僕らのこと identifies those being made to laugh; the object marker を is omitted.

5.3.n: 笑わせる means make someone laugh; てくれる presents this as something welcome that he does for them.

5.4.n: し adds another reason supporting the speaker's praise.

6.0.n: 本当に emphasizes that the speaker sincerely holds this opinion.

6.2.n: すごく is the く-form of すごい, used here to strengthen いい.

6.3.n: いい directly describes 監督 and expresses the speaker's positive judgment.

6.4.n: 監督 refers to Shinjo's role leading the team.

6.5.n: だ is the plain counterpart of です, used inside the thought being reported.

6.6.n: な adds a reflective, appreciative tone to the speaker's inner judgment.

6.7.n: と marks the preceding judgment as the content of 思ってます.

6.8.n: 思ってます shortens 思っています, a polite form expressing an opinion the speaker currently holds.

0.tip: Japanese introductions commonly omit I and put the family name before the given name.

1.lit: As for Shinjo, manager, is kind?
1.tip: A title such as 監督 follows the person's name in Japanese.

2.lit: As for Shinjo, manager, you know, kind, I tell you. Very.
2.tip: めっちゃ comes after the statement as a casual, emphatic afterthought.

3.lit: Um, in media and such, strictly, you know, he does things like say harsh things, but...
3.tip: では contrasts his behavior in the media with his behavior toward the players.

4.lit: Really, as for when he talks with us, he always offers kind words for us, and...
4.tip: てくれる shows that the speaker welcomes or appreciates what someone does for him or his group.

5.lit: He makes us laugh for us, and...
5.tip: し lists another reason for the speaker's positive view of the manager.

6.lit: Really, a very good manager he is, indeed, I think.
6.tip: と marks the whole preceding judgment as what the speaker thinks.
